subject.title: You Know All This
subject.author: Kenneth Koch
subject.text:
The first, violent year
 I could not swim or float;
A dark and balanced fear
  Hung on me like a coat.

The second year it rained,
  The rain was strict and odd;
The fur of fear remained
  But I whistled Scheherazade.

The summer of the third
  I stripped with some dispatch;
Still finding me absurd
  You struck me like a match:

Flaming, naked, stung,
  I held you for a year,
Persistent as a tongue,
  Infecting you, my dear.

My hands, somnambular,
  Have kept you like a vow;
No matter where you are
  We touch each other now.

title: Whistling Scheherazade in the Rain
standfirst: Kenneth Koch is remembered as the fastest, funniest voice to come out of the New York School. In August 1948, five years before any of that reputation existed, Poetry printed five plain, correctly rhymed quatrains by a 23-year-old barely out of Harvard, about the three years it took him to let somebody touch him.

sections.heading: Not the Voice You'd Recognize
sections.body:
Ask someone who knows Kenneth Koch's later work to describe him and you will get some version of: fast, comic, allergic to solemnity, the poet who could turn a Renaissance painting or a grocery run into a running joke he was clearly enjoying more than you were. None of that is in "You Know All This." Five short, alternately rhymed quatrains, addressed without a single wisecrack to somebody the poem never names. Strip the byline and Koch would be near the bottom of anyone's guess.

For four stanzas the rhymes do their job without strain: *float/coat*, *rained/remained*, *third/absurd*, *dispatch/match*, *stung/tongue*, *year/dear*. Only once in that stretch does the machinery show effort — when "odd" has to reach all the way to "Scheherazade" to close a stanza, the poem's one visible risk, landing on its strangest image. The fifth stanza gives up on the pattern altogether, which is where this piece ends.

sections.heading: A Year Named by Its Weather
sections.body:
The poem counts itself out in years, and gives each one a single dominant fact rather than a scene. Year one: he could not swim or float, and fear sat on him "like a coat." Year two arrives as weather:

> The second year it rained,
>   The rain was strict and odd;
> The fur of fear remained
>   But I whistled Scheherazade.

"Strict and odd" rain is a small, exact piece of noticing — rain with a temperament — but it is the next line that does the real work. Whistling a piece of orchestral music at fear is a defense with no dignity and no explanation offered for it, and the poem doesn't try to supply one. Year three finally moves: "I stripped with some dispatch," and the other person, still finding him absurd, "struck me like a match." The whole poem turns on that verb — not warmed, not lit, *struck*, with the violence carried over from the coat of fear in line one.

sections.heading: Already a Published Poet at Twenty
sections.body:
Koch had left home at eighteen to serve in the Pacific theater of the Second World War, and went to Harvard on his return, according to the Adrian Brinkerhoff Poetry Foundation's account of his life. It was at Harvard that he met John Ashbery, the beginning of the friendship that would later be filed, along with Frank O'Hara, under "the New York School" — though that name and its reputation for exuberant, anti-confessional cosmopolitanism, as the Academy of American Poets describes it, belonged to the 1950s, not yet to a Harvard undergraduate finishing his degree.

He was not a beginner sending out his first envelope. The Kenneth Koch Papers at the New York Public Library record an earlier poem, "The Trip from California," already published in *Poetry* in November 1945 — Koch would have been twenty. By the time he wrote "You Know All This," he had several years of practice at being read by strangers, which may be one reason the poem is so careful to make its argument in complete, correctly punctuated sentences rather than risk anything.

sections.heading: Revised Across the Move to New York
sections.body: The New York Public Library's finding aid for Koch's papers lists the manuscript plainly, under its full working title: "You know all this (The first, violent year)," three drafts, the second dated July 1947 and the third 1948. That single line pins the poem to a specific stretch of Koch's life more precisely than anything else available. He drafted it as a Harvard undergraduate in the summer of 1947, then kept revising it through 1948 — the year he graduated and moved to New York to begin doctoral work at Columbia, by his own later account and the Academy of American Poets' summary of his career. Whatever the poem's "violent year" was describing, its author was rewriting the line describing it while packing up one city for another.

sections.heading: Company in the August Issue
sections.body: "You Know All This" appeared in *Poetry* in August 1948 — volume 72, number 5, page 13, per the magazine's own archive. It ran alongside four poems by Weldon Kees, work by Peter Viereck, and a page of poets — Thomas Barbour, Desmond Stewart, Elliott Coleman among them — whose names now belong mainly to specialists. Nothing in that table of contents marks Koch out. He reads, in this company, like a competent young formalist keeping pace with a fairly conventional literary magazine, which is exactly what he was, five years before Tibor de Nagy Gallery put his name next to Nell Blaine's and started a fight.

sections.heading: Five Years Later, Called Dull
sections.body:
In 1953 the Tibor de Nagy Gallery published *Poems*, Koch's first book — three hundred numbered copies, Nell Blaine's color block prints tipped into the pages alongside his verse, an early entry in what would become a whole run of poet-painter collaborations out of that gallery. The critic Harry Roskolenko reviewed it in *Poetry*, the same magazine that had printed "You Know All This" without incident, and did not like it: Koch's writing was "tasteless, futile, noisy and dull," his verse "lazy," "precious and puerile," barely "the bric-a-brac of poetry."

Frank O'Hara answered him in the same pages, arguing that Koch had "the other poetic gift: vivacity and go, originality of perception and intoxication with life," and — turning Roskolenko's own word back on him — insisting that "most important of all, he is not dull." Read next to that fight, "You Know All This" looks like a different poet's work: patient, formally obedient, in no hurry to be original. Something changed in the five years between the quiet debut and the noisy one, and neither review mentions the earlier poem at all.

sections.heading: The Rhyme That Gives Up
sections.body:
The poem's last stanza is where its discipline finally slips:

> My hands, somnambular,
>   Have kept you like a vow;
> No matter where you are
>   We touch each other now.

Every earlier stanza rhymes its first line with its third. Here it doesn't — "somnambular" and "are" share nothing but a stray vowel. Only the second pair, "vow" and "now," still closes cleanly. It is a small thing, and it may be nothing more than a poet running out of patience four stanzas in. But it happens exactly where the poem stops narrating the past — first year, second year, third year, "I held you for a year" — and drops into a present tense it cannot fully explain: two people who touch "no matter where" they are, for reasons and across a distance the poem never specifies.

Nothing in the archive names who "you" was. The finding aid records drafts and dates, not people. So the poem ends the way its own last rhyme does — reaching for a match that almost, not quite, arrives.
